# Customer Inquiry Intake

An RFQ is a customer asking *what would this cost, and when could I have it?*

In make-to-order manufacturing there is **no standard format**, and the
estimator's first job is always the same one: extract the specs, quantities,
dates and terms into a consistent shape, and work out what is missing. That
extraction is mechanical, high-volume, and currently done by the most expensive
person in the department.

**Quick start**

```
→ Ingest everything as ONE inquiry, however many attachments arrived
→ Extract into the intake form; every field cites its file and page
→ Per line: what geometry arrived, and its path (C2 drawing, C1 STEP, B prior part, A text, none). A text-only line is a ROM at most
→ Per tolerance: how it was read. A general note applied to a feature is reading, and cites the note
→ Split what was never stated from what was stated two ways. Two registers
→ Check manufacturability FIRST. A hard disqualifier stops here, before we ask the customer anything
→ Draft the questions back as a sendable email, not a checklist
→ Recommend bid or no-bid PROVISIONALLY — never wait for answers; name which answer would change it
→ Answers re-enter at extract, not at scoring. Re-score and say what moved
→ No reply? Surface as stale. Stale never cancels, declines or closes
→ Never infer a tolerance. Never decide. Recommend
→ Stop at the registers, the questions and the bid/no-bid. No hours, no cycle times, no costing — that is quote-build's
```

## Workflow

### Step 1 — Ingest

**First, look for it on the Open work page.** Before building a form, look
for the RFQ reference (or the customer and part) in `## Open inquiries`
(`../../shared/replies.md`, *The open work*). If it is there, resume that form

answer pasted into a new chat with nothing attached is enough to resume.

Accept an email with attachments, a folder, or a pasted document.

**A multi-attachment RFQ is one inquiry with several line items, never several

Detect whether this revises an earlier RFQ and **link rather than duplicate**.

Header, line items, quantities as a structure, specs, dates, commercial terms.

# How an RFQ actually arrives

**There is no standard format, and that is exactly the problem this skill
exists to solve.** In one week an estimator might get all five of these.

The extraction is mechanical, high-volume work, and it is currently done by the
most expensive person in the department.

---

## The five formats

### 1. A PDF drawing package with "can you do this?" in the email body

The commercial terms are often in the email, the technical content in the
attachments. The email body is an input, not a covering note.

### 2. A spreadsheet with 40 line items and no drawings

The column headers are the customer's. Extract what is there. Do not invent
drawings that did not arrive.

### 3. A customer portal export with fields in an unfamiliar order

The field names are the portal's, not yours. Extract into the intake form
anyway.

Portal exports carry a generation timestamp. **Note it** — a portal export
pulled a week ago may no longer match what the portal says today, and the
response deadline is usually counted from the portal's date rather than the
day the file reached you.

### 4. A phone photo of a marked-up print

Extract what is visible and **mark the line for human review**.

**Never infer a tolerance from a drawing**, and never from a photograph of one.
A `specs` entry with no source reference is not permitted.

### 5. A forwarded thread where the requirement is in the fourth message down

Read the thread. Cite the message each field came from. Do not treat the latest
message as the requirement just because it is latest.

---

**A multi-attachment RFQ is one inquiry with several line items, never several
inquiries.**

Different parts in one package can carry different delivery dates, different
quantities and different certifications. That is normal — the contract holds
dates per line for exactly this reason. Splitting the package into separate
inquiries loses the fact that the customer is asking for them together, which is
often the whole commercial point.

---

## Revisions of an earlier RFQ

Detect and **link** rather than creating a duplicate. Set `supersedes_rfq`.

A revised RFQ that quietly becomes a second inquiry is how a plant ends up
quoting the same job twice against different requirements, then sending both.

Signals worth checking: the customer's own reference reappearing, the same part
and customer within a short window, "revised," "updated," or "rev 2" in a
filename or subject line.

Every extracted field carries **which file and which page it came from**, so the
estimator can verify without re-reading the package.

This is what separates a useful extraction from one that has to be checked from
scratch, and it is why `field_sources` is a required field the consumer blocks
on. An estimator who cannot trace a number will re-derive all of them, and the
skill has then saved nobody anything.

**The ordering is the point, twice over.** The constraint check runs *before*
the questions go out and *before* the bid/no-bid call — so a job that cannot be
built as specified is caught at intake rather than after somebody has spent
hours pricing it, and the plant never asks a customer five questions about a
part it physically cannot make.

---

Quoting is expensive — often hours of the most senior person in the department.
**Quoting a job you will lose, or one you should not want, is pure cost.**

Wrong material, a tolerance the plant has never held, a size outside the
envelope, an impossible date: each of those is a job that either does not get
won, or gets won and then loses money. A defensible no-bid returns those hours
to the RFQs that can be won.

---

From the capability profile captured during `onboarding`: materials, processes,
size envelope, demonstrated tolerance capability, certifications held.

**Report each violated constraint specifically**, never as a general fail:

> *"True position of 0.0005 in on the 4x mounting holes is below this plant's
> demonstrated capability on 3-axis milling, which is 0.002 in. Everything else
> on this line — 6061-T6, the envelope, clear anodize — is within profile."*

That is a sentence an estimator can act on. They may know the plant can hold it
on a different machine, or that the customer will accept a deviation, or that

none of that** and sends them back to work out which constraint failed.

Some violations end the automated sequence at the check rather than feeding the

estimate how long it takes to make.** It is an estimating aid. It is not the
